source.visualizer: Greg Shirah (NASA/GSFC), Horace Mitchell (NASA/GSFC); scientists Atousa Saberi (NASA/GSFC), Josh Willis (JPL)
source.dataset: ECCO2 high-resolution ocean and sea ice model (NASA/JPL); Blue Marble: Next Generation

frames.label: The whole ocean
frames.place: the whole Earth as it turns
frames.alt: The Earth turning slowly, its oceans covered in fine white streaks of moving water; the brightest bands run along the equator and the coasts of continents.
frames.story: The whole planet turns beneath you. Every white streak is water on the move. Listen for the bright bands hugging the east coasts of continents: those are the great western boundary currents, and the tour is about to visit three of them.

frames.label: Kuroshio Current, off Japan
frames.place: the Kuroshio, south and east of Japan
frames.alt: Close view south of Japan: a bright white river of current hugs the coast, then breaks into loops and swirls as it heads east into the Pacific.
frames.story: The Kuroshio, the "Black Current", carries warm tropical water north past Japan. Where it leaves the coast it starts to meander and throw off eddies, swirls hundreds of kilometres across. Busy, ringing notes mean a strong, tangled current.

frames.label: Across Asia and the Indian Ocean
frames.ariaLabel: Across Asia and the Indian Ocean
frames.place: Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean
frames.alt: The camera pulls back and the globe turns past Southeast Asia and Australia to the Indian Ocean.
frames.story: The camera pulls back and travels west over Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean. Quieter stretches here are calmer open water.

frames.label: Agulhas Current, off South Africa
frames.place: the Agulhas, off the southern tip of Africa
frames.alt: Close view of southern Africa: a strong current runs down the east coast, turns back at the tip of the continent, and sheds bright round rings that drift west into the Atlantic.
frames.story: The Agulhas runs down Africa's east coast and, at the tip of the continent, turns back on itself. As it turns it pinches off rings of warm, salty Indian Ocean water that drift into the Atlantic. Each ring that crosses the line rings a note: you are hearing two oceans connect.

frames.label: Across the South Atlantic
frames.place: the South Atlantic, towards South America
frames.alt: The camera crosses the open South Atlantic towards Brazil; scattered rings and soft streaks over dark blue water.
frames.story: The camera crosses the South Atlantic, following the path of those rings towards South America and then north. Open ocean is mostly a quiet, low drone.

frames.label: Gulf Stream, off the United States
frames.ariaLabel: Gulf Stream, off the United States
frames.place: the Gulf Stream, off the east coast of the United States
frames.alt: Close view of the east coast of the United States: a thick white current leaves Florida, runs north along the coast, then swings out into the Atlantic in huge meanders and eddies.
frames.story: The Gulf Stream leaves Florida, runs up the coast and swings out into the Atlantic in giant meanders. It carries warmth towards Europe. Scientists watch this circulation closely, because a warming climate may be slowing the Atlantic's overturning circulation it is part of. This is the loudest, busiest part of the tour.

frames.label: Gulf of Mexico and the Loop Current
frames.ariaLabel: Gulf of Mexico and the Loop Current
frames.place: the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean
frames.alt: Close view of the Gulf of Mexico: a current loops up from the Caribbean, curls around and sheds large eddies before leaving past Florida.
frames.story: In the Gulf of Mexico the Loop Current pushes up from the Caribbean, curls around and sheds large eddies, then leaves past Florida to feed the Gulf Stream. Warm eddies like these can strengthen hurricanes that pass over them.

frames.label: The whole ocean again
frames.place: the whole Earth as it turns
frames.alt: The camera pulls back to the whole Earth over the Americas, oceans streaked with white currents.
frames.story: The camera pulls back. Every current you heard is one connected system, moving heat around the planet. The tour ends almost three years after it began.

legend.summary: NASA's tour of the ocean's currents, January 2021 to December 2023: the whole globe, then the Kuroshio, the Agulhas and the Gulf Stream. A line runs top to bottom through the middle of the picture, and you hear the moving water that crosses it.
legend.method: The top of the picture sounds higher and in your left ear; the bottom lower and in your right. Calm, open water is a soft, low swell. Where strong currents and eddies cross the line, a harp rings and the swell grows. A soft low pulse marks the start of each month.

items.meaning: A strong current or an eddy crossing the line. Louder = brighter, faster water.
All the moving water on the line. It is soft over calm ocean and grows over strong currents.
A soft low pulse at the start of each month, so you can hear time passing.

legend.caveat: Values are read from the brightness of NASA's white flow lines, which show currents in the top 600 metres (deeper flows, drawn in blue, are not read). They are relative, not speeds in metres per second. The camera moves, so the line crosses different places as the tour goes on; the scenes name where it is.
